questionText:
For constants $a \ge 1$ and $b > 1$, consider the following recurrence defined on the non-negative integers:

$$T(n) = a \cdot T\left(\frac{n}{b}\right) + f(n)$$

Which one of the following options is correct about the recurrence $T(n)$?
options: If $f(n)$ is $O(n^{\log_b(a) - \epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon > 0$, then $T(n)$ is $\Theta(n^{\log_b(a)})$.
explanation:
According to Case 1 of the Master Theorem for divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form $T(n) = a \cdot T\left(\frac{n}{b}\right) + f(n)$ where $a \ge 1$ and $b > 1$:

If $f(n) = O(n^{\log_b(a) - \epsilon})$ for some constant $\epsilon > 0$, then the work done at the leaves dominates the overall recurrence time complexity, giving:
$$T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b(a)})$$

Thus, statement (C) is a direct formulation of Case 1 of the Master Theorem and is correct.

Analysis of other options:
• Option (A) & (B): The exact growth order depends on the specific values of $a$ and $b$, so general statements cannot be made without knowing $a$ and $b$.
• Option (D): If $f(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b(a)})$, this corresponds to Case 2 of the Master Theorem, which yields $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b(a)} \log n)$ instead of $\Theta(n^{\log_b(a)})$.
